624.title: One man for the people (John 11:45–57)
624.hook: the council plots; Caiaphas says it's better one man die
624.howItsDone: Many churches pray for those in authority in their regular services; Christians read Caiaphas's words as an unknowing prophecy that Jesus would die for many.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus wept at a tomb, then called Lazarus out, still wrapped in grave clothes. Your line was loose him, let him go. What did you help unwrap? Day six hundred twenty-four.

A room, worried people, and someone saying the hard, practical thing out loud. That's today's scene. After Lazarus walks out of the tomb, many who saw it believe. Some go to Jerusalem and report what happened. And the chief priests and leaders call an emergency meeting of the council. Their question is a frightened one, and very human: "What do we? for this man doeth many miracles." They're not debating whether the miracle happened. They're asking what it will cost them.

To understand the room, you have to understand the pressure on it. Judea was under Roman occupation. Rome let the temple and its leaders keep a measure of authority, as long as there was order. Crowds, excitement, talk of a king: that was exactly what Rome crushed. The council says it plainly: "If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him: and the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation." Their fear wasn't imaginary. Decades later, Roman armies did destroy the temple. Then the high priest that year, Caiaphas, speaks. "Ye know nothing at all, nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not." Expedient means better, useful, the practical choice. One life traded for many. It's an old logic: sacrifice one to keep the peace. And then John does something remarkable. He says Caiaphas spoke better than he knew. Being high priest, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, "and not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad." The same sentence, heard two ways. Caiaphas meant politics. John hears the gospel in it: one man dying for the people, gathering the scattered. From that day, John says, they made plans. Jesus withdraws to a town called Ephraim, near the wilderness. Passover is near, and the whole city is wondering: will he come to the feast? It was Rome that would carry out the execution. But the road toward it begins in a frightened room.
screen: then, large: `ONE MAN SHOULD DIE FOR THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold leaders under pressure in mind. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who makes hard decisions for others. A mayor, a head of state, a school principal, a hospital director, a manager at work. Imagine the weight of their room: competing fears, real dangers, people who'll be hurt either way. You don't have to agree with them. Just picture them as people under pressure. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, for wisdom and courage, and that no one is sacrificed for convenience. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with honesty and fairness. The bell holds the time.
Caiaphas. The high priest who said one man should die for the people, which John hears as an unknowing prophecy of Jesus's death.
Your line: for the nation. Today, when you hear news about a leader's hard decision, pause and ask who pays the price for it. Day six hundred twenty-four.

625.title: The house filled with fragrance (John 12:1–11)
625.hook: Mary anoints his feet and wipes them with her hair
625.tomorrow: unless a grain of wheat falls
625.howItsDone: Christians read Mary's anointing in Holy Week in many churches; in some traditions, fragrant oil is used to anoint at baptism, confirmation and healing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a frightened council and Caiaphas saying one man should die for the people. Your line was for the nation. Who did you hold in mind under pressure? Day six hundred twenty-five.

One breath of a certain soap, a certain bread, a certain perfume, and you can be seven years old again, or standing next to someone you lost. Six days before Passover, Jesus comes back to Bethany, to the house of the friends he loves. They give him a dinner. Martha serves, of course. Lazarus, who was dead and buried not long ago, is sitting at the table, eating. And then Mary gets up, carrying something.

"Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair: and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment." Spikenard, or nard, is an oil made from a plant that grows high in the Himalayas. It had to travel thousands of miles to reach a village in Judea. A Roman pound is about twelve ounces, a great deal of perfume. Honored guests were sometimes anointed on the head. Mary goes to his feet. And wipes them with her hair. A woman letting down her hair in front of guests was a striking thing in that world. She doesn't seem to care. Then the whole house smells of it, and John is the Gospel writer who notices that. Judas objects, and his question sounds reasonable: "Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor?" Three hundred denarii, about a year's wages for a laborer. John adds that Judas kept the money bag and helped himself from it. Jesus answers: "Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this." Mary is anointing a body for burial while it's still alive. She seems to understand what's coming better than anyone at the table. One more detail. Christians in the West have sometimes blended this Mary with Mary Magdalene and with an unnamed woman in Luke's Gospel. Eastern churches kept them separate, and since its 1969 reform the Catholic calendar treats them as different women. John simply calls her Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus.
screen: then, large: `THE HOUSE WAS FILLED WITH THE ODOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wear or smell something fragrant. If there's something with a scent near you, soap, a spice, a flower, coffee, lotion, bring it close. If not, remember one. Settle, and breathe. Breathe in slowly through your nose. Let the scent fill you. Notice what it brings back, or who. Then think of someone you love, and imagine giving them something extravagant, not useful, just beautiful, because they matter. If you pray, you can offer this moment to God as Mary offered the nard. If you don't, simply breathe in the scent with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Nard. The costly oil, also called spikenard, that Mary poured on Jesus's feet, until the whole house smelled of it.
Your line: the house was filled. Today, do one extravagant, unnecessary, loving thing for someone, the kind that fills a room. Day six hundred twenty-five.

626.title: Unless a grain of wheat falls (John 12:12–26)
626.hook: a seed must fall into the earth and die to bear much fruit
626.howItsDone: Christians remember the entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday, often carrying palms; the grain of wheat saying is often read at funerals and in Holy Week.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary poured nard on Jesus's feet in Bethany, and the house was filled with the scent. Your line was the house was filled. What extravagant thing did you do? Day six hundred twenty-six.

The next day, the city is packed for Passover, and word spreads that Jesus is coming. A great crowd goes out to meet him. John tells us what they carried: "Took branches of palm trees, and went forth to meet him, and cried, Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord." Hosanna is a Hebrew cry, save us, now. Jesus finds a young donkey and rides in on it. The religious leaders watch the crowds and say to one another: "behold, the world is gone after him." And then, as if to prove them right, some Greeks arrive.

These Greeks are pilgrims, outsiders who have come up to worship at the feast. They go to Philip and ask politely: "Sir, we would see Jesus." Philip tells Andrew, and together they tell Jesus. You'd expect him to say, bring them in. Instead, he says the hour has come. And then he talks about a seed. "Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." Corn, in the King James Bible, means any grain: here, a single grain of wheat. Kept in a jar, it stays a grain forever. Safe, whole, and alone. Planted, buried in the dark, it breaks open and stops being a seed. And then it becomes a stalk heavy with grain. Jesus is talking about his own death. The Greeks want to see him, and his answer is: the way the world will see me is through my dying. One grain becomes a harvest. Then he widens it to everyone who follows him: "He that loveth his life shall lose it." Not a call to despise life, but to let go of clutching it. The verse has traveled. Dostoevsky put it at the front of The Brothers Karamazov, as the epigraph for the whole book. Farmers know it without any book: you can't eat your seed grain and have a harvest too. Christians often read these words at funerals, and whenever something has to end so something else can begin.
screen: `A GRAIN IN A JAR STAYS ALONE.`
then, large: `EXCEPT A CORN OF WHEAT FALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one thing go. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been holding onto too tightly. An old plan that isn't working. A grudge. A version of yourself you've outgrown. A role, a possession, a need to be right. Hold it like a seed in your palm. Notice how hard you're gripping. Then imagine opening your hand and letting it fall into the ground. You don't have to know what will grow from it. If you pray, you can place it in God's hands. If you don't, simply notice what your open hand feels like. The bell holds the time.
Grain. A single seed of wheat, Jesus says, that must fall into the ground and die before it can bear much fruit.
Your line: unless it dies. Today, let one small thing go on purpose, and leave room for what might grow. Day six hundred twenty-six.

627.title: Walk while you have light (John 12:27–50)
627.hook: now is my soul troubled; walk while you have the light
627.tomorrow: he loved them to the end
627.howItsDone: Christians often read this passage in Holy Week; some pray at sunset, keeping the evening as a time to remember the light while it lasts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Greeks asked to see Jesus, and he talked about a grain of wheat. Your line was unless it dies. What did you let go of? Day six hundred twenty-seven.

Late afternoon light goes gold and long, and there's maybe an hour before dark. Anything you meant to do outside, you'd better do now. Farmers know it. Kids playing in the street know it. Today's passage is the late afternoon of Jesus's public life in John's Gospel. After this, he won't speak to the crowds again. Everything from chapter thirteen on happens in private, with his closest friends, and then on the way to the cross. So these are his last public words. And he begins by admitting something.

"Now is my soul troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto this hour." He's troubled, and says so. The other Gospels show it in the garden of Gethsemane; John shows it here. And instead of asking to be spared, he prays: "Father, glorify thy name." Then a voice comes from heaven: "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again." The crowd hears it differently. Some say it thundered. Others say an angel spoke. The same sound, and people hear what they're ready to hear. Then he says, "And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me." Lifted up: on a cross, and, as John hears it, into glory, both at once. And then comes today's line, with the urgency of sunset: "Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you." It's not a threat. It's what someone says to a friend when the sun is going down: don't wait. While the light is here, use it. "While ye have light, believe in the light, that ye may be the children of light." Then, John says, he went away and hid himself. Before the curtain falls on the public ministry, Jesus cries out a summary of everything he's said. And it ends gently. He says he came not to judge the world, but to save the world. Some readers call John chapters one to twelve the Book of Signs. Tomorrow, a new part begins.
screen: then, large: `WALK WHILE YE HAVE THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one good thing before dark. Settle, and breathe. Picture today's light. Where is the sun right now? Morning, noon, already going down? Then think of one good thing you've been putting off. A call to an aging parent. An apology. A thank-you note. Visiting someone. Something that won't wait forever. Picture doing it today, while there's still light. Notice any reluctance, and how small it is next to the thing itself. If you pray, you can ask for help to do it. If you don't, simply choose the hour you'll do it. The bell holds the time.
Gethsemane. The garden where the other Gospels show Jesus's trouble of soul; John shows that same trouble here instead, in his last public words.
Your line: while you have the light. Today, do the good thing you chose before the sun goes down. Day six hundred twenty-seven.

628.title: He loved them to the end (John 13:1–17)
628.hook: he washes the feet of every disciple, even Judas
628.howItsDone: Some churches wash feet on Holy Thursday, the evening before Good Friday; some Mennonite and Brethren churches practice footwashing regularly, and others keep the command through acts of humble service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus's last public words in John, his trouble like the one in Gethsemane, at sunset. Your line was while you have the light. What good thing did you do before dark? Day six hundred twenty-eight.

Sandals, dirt roads, donkeys and sheep. Arrive at a dinner in Jesus's world and your feet would be filthy. A host might offer water, and the washing was a servant's job. Now it's the evening before Passover. Jesus and his friends are already at supper, and the dust of the road is still on their feet. Nobody has washed anyone's feet. And John opens a new part of his Gospel with one sentence.

"Now before the feast of the passover, when Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father, having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end." Unto the end can mean two things in Greek. To the last moment, and also to the uttermost, completely. Both are true here. Then Jesus gets up from supper, takes off his outer robe, and ties a towel around his waist, dressed like a servant. "After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded." Picture the room going silent. When he gets to Peter, Peter refuses: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." It's wrong, it's upside down. Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." And Peter swings to the opposite extreme: "Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head." From never to everything, in two breaths. Then a detail John doesn't hide. John has just told us that the devil had already put it into Judas's heart to betray him. And Jesus knows. He says so: not all of you are clean. And he washes every disciple's feet anyway. Including the feet that will walk out of this room to betray him. When he's done, he puts his robe back on and says: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." Churches keep this command differently. Some Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches wash feet in the Holy Thursday service. Some Mennonite and Brethren churches wash feet regularly as an ordinance. Others hear it mainly as a call to humble service.
screen: `TO THE LAST, AND TO THE UTTERMOST.`
then, large: `HE LOVED THEM UNTO THE END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve someone you find difficult. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's hard for you. Not dangerous, just difficult. A coworker who grates on you, a relative you avoid, someone who let you down. Picture them clearly. Now picture yourself doing one small, humble thing for them. Making their coffee. Helping with a task. Saying something kind about them to someone else. Notice the resistance in you. Let it be there. If you pray, you can ask for the humility to serve them anyway. If you don't, simply hold the picture for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Towel. What Jesus tied around his waist, dressed like a servant, before he knelt to wash every disciple's feet.
Your line: to the end. Today, do the one humble thing you pictured for the difficult person, and don't mention it. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

629.title: The one he loved (John 13:18–30)
629.hook: the beloved disciple leans on his chest; Judas goes out, and it was night
629.howItsDone: Christians remember this supper on Maundy or Holy Thursday; church tradition honors the beloved disciple as Saint John the Evangelist, while some scholars hold the question of his identity open.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a towel and a basin, and Jesus washing every disciple's feet. Your line was to the end. Did you serve someone difficult? Day six hundred twenty-nine.

Forget the famous painting. In Leonardo's Last Supper, everyone sits in a row on one side of a long table, like a panel at a conference. At a formal dinner in Jesus's world, guests often reclined. Low couches around a low table, each guest propped on one elbow, feet stretched out behind. In that arrangement, the person next to you is close, your head near their chest. That's the scene tonight. Jesus has just washed their feet. And now he becomes deeply troubled and says something that stops the meal.

"Verily, verily, I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me." The disciples look at each other, not knowing whom he means. And John introduces someone new, someone John hasn't named this way before: "Now there was leaning on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved." The beloved disciple. John's Gospel never gives his name. He appears at the cross, at the empty tomb, by the lake, and at the very end the Gospel says this disciple is the one who wrote these things down. Who was he? Church tradition, as early as the writer Irenaeus, says John, the son of Zebedee. Some modern scholars suggest someone else: Lazarus, whom the sisters called he whom thou lovest, or a disciple from Jerusalem outside the twelve. Nobody can prove it. The Gospel keeps his name quiet, maybe on purpose, so any reader can lean into that place. There's an echo here. The word for bosom is the same word used in chapter one, where the Son is in the bosom of the Father. As Jesus rests close to the Father, this disciple rests close to Jesus. Peter nudges him: ask who it is. He leans back and asks. Jesus says: the one I give this piece of bread to, after I've dipped it. And he gives it to Judas. Some readers see the morsel as a host's mark of honor. If so, even now, Jesus offers him friendship. Then: "That thou doest, do quickly." The others think Judas is going to buy something for the feast, or give to the poor. And the line John ends the scene on: "He then having received the sop went immediately out: and it was night."

Here's the practice: lean on someone you trust. Settle, and breathe. Let your body lean into whatever is holding you: the back of a chair, a wall, the floor. Let it take your weight. Notice how much effort you usually spend holding yourself up. Then think of a person you trust enough to lean on. Someone you could tell the truth to, or ask for help. Picture leaning on them a little, the way the beloved disciple leaned back to ask a hard question. If you pray, you can rest in God the same way. If you don't, simply let yourself be held. The bell holds the time.
Beloved disciple. The unnamed disciple whom Jesus loved, who leaned on his chest at supper, and whom John's Gospel names as its witness.
Your line: and it was night. Today, before night comes, reach out to the person you trust and lean on them a little, even with one honest sentence. Day six hundred twenty-nine.

630.title: A new commandment (John 13:31–38)
630.hook: love one another as I have loved you; by this all will know
630.howItsDone: Christians remember the new commandment on Maundy Thursday, often with footwashing, communion and the stripping of the altar; many churches also take it as the measure of their common life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beloved disciple leaned on Jesus's chest, and Judas took the bread and went out. Your line was and it was night. Who did you lean on? Day six hundred thirty.

Ever wonder why the Thursday before Easter is called Maundy Thursday? Maundy is an odd word. Outside this one week, English hardly uses it. It comes from Latin. In the old Latin Bible, today's verse begins with the words mandatum novum, a new commandment. Mandatum became maundy. So a whole day of the Christian year is named after one sentence Jesus spoke at supper, right after Judas walked out into the night. The door has just closed behind him. The room is quieter now. And Jesus speaks to the eleven who are left, like a father at the end.

He calls them little children, the only time in John's Gospel he does, and tells them he's going where they can't follow yet. Then: "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another." Love one another isn't new on its own. The law of Moses already says, love thy neighbor as thyself. Jesus himself quoted it. So what's new? The measure. As I have loved you. Not as you love yourself, but as he has loved them, and they've just seen what that looks like: a towel, a basin, and feet, including the feet of the one who left. Then the sign: "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." Not by a badge, a building, or a set of correct opinions. By love they can see. Around the year two hundred, a Christian writer in North Africa named Tertullian reported what outsiders said about the Christians they knew: see how they love one another. Then Peter interrupts. Lord, where are you going? Why can't I follow you now? "I will lay down my life for thy sake." He means it. And Jesus answers with sad honesty: "The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice." Even the friend who promises the most will fail tonight. The new commandment is given to people who will need it. Look back over this week: a frightened council, nard filling a house, a grain of wheat, walking in the light, a towel and basin, a disciple leaning close, and now love as the sign.
screen: `PETER: I WILL LAY DOWN MY LIFE.`
then, large: `AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love someone visibly. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone in your life whose love for you has been visible. Not just felt, but seen. Something they did. Remember it clearly. Now think of someone you love, but maybe not visibly enough. A friend, a family member, someone in your community. What could you do today that they would actually see? Not a big gesture. A note, a meal, an hour, showing up. Picture it. If you pray, you can ask to love as you've been loved. If you don't, simply decide on the one thing. The bell holds the time.
Tertullian. A Christian writer in North Africa who reported what outsiders said of believers: see how they love one another.
Your line: by this, all will know. Today, do the one visible act of love you chose, where it can be seen by the person it's for. Day six hundred thirty, and another week on the path.

myth: love your neighbor was first commanded by Jesus
it's in the law of Moses, Leviticus 19:18. the new part is "as I have loved you."
Maundy comes from the Latin word for commandment
mandatum novum, a new commandment.
Peter promised to lay down his life for Jesus
and Jesus told him he'd deny him three times before the rooster crowed.

fork.setup: you're Peter. Jesus says he's going where you can't follow yet. what do you say?
options: "I will lay down my life for thy sake."
fork.reveal: Peter means it. Jesus answers: "the cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice."

original.note: Greek: new, fresh. A new commandment: the old command to love, with a new measure.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus invented the command to love one another.
what it means: the command to love is old; what's new is the measure, as I have loved you, shown with a towel and a basin.
what a scholar hears: the Latin mandatum novum gave English Maundy Thursday, and Tertullian reports outsiders saying, see how they love one another.
